title: Zinfandel
description: Also called Primitivo in Italy and Tribidrag in Croatia. Ripe bramble fruit, high alcohol and a long American story.
L: Zinfandel gives ripe, often jammy wines with blackberry, raspberry, bramble, black pepper and sweet spice, sometimes dried fruit. Alcohol is often high, 14.5 to 16%. Tannins are moderate, acidity medium. The style can range from light rosé to rich, powerful reds and sweet wines.

Zinfandel's bunches ripen unevenly: some berries are still green while others shrivel into raisins. Growers must wait for most to ripen, by which time some are overripe. That raises sugar and alcohol, and gives the mix of fresh and dried fruit flavours. It's also why picking time is so critical.
Green berries and raisins on one bunch
Why is Zinfandel often high in alcohol?
Uneven ripening means some berries shrivel and concentrate sugar
Waiting for the green berries to ripen leaves others overripe, raising sugar and alcohol.

Look for medium to deep colour, ripe bramble and jammy berry fruit, black pepper and sweet spice, a warm, high-alcohol feel and moderate tannin. A hint of dried fruit or raisin is typical. It's fruitier and less tannic than Cabernet, spicier than Merlot.
Zinfandel is medium to deep in colour, not pale.
Zinfandel gives ripe bramble fruit, spice and high alcohol
Uneven ripening mixes fresh and raisined berries
It ranges from rosé to rich red and sweet styles
Name its homes in Italy and Croatia

Zinfandel reached the United States in the 1820s, from an Austrian nursery collection. It spread through California during the Gold Rush and became the state's most widely planted red for decades. Today it's grown in Lodi, Sonoma's Dry Creek Valley, Amador County in the Sierra Foothills, and Paso Robles.

In Italy it's called Primitivo, grown in Puglia, especially Manduria and Gioia del Colle. Primitivo means early one, because it ripens early. Its origin is Croatia, where it's called Tribidrag or Crljenak Kaštelanski, and today grows in small amounts on the Dalmatian coast.
Primitivo in Puglia; origin in Croatia
Match each name to its country.
One grape with three national identities.

Zinfandel likes warm, sunny climates with dry autumns, which help with its uneven ripening. Cool, damp weather causes rot in its tight bunches. Many of its best wines come from old, head-trained vines, grown without trellises, which give low yields and concentrated fruit.
Primitivo refers to its early ripening.
It's Primitivo in Puglia and Tribidrag in Croatia
It likes warm, dry climates and old head-trained vines
Explain how Zinfandel and Primitivo were linked
Explain how its Croatian origin was found

For years, Zinfandel was thought to be an American grape. In the 1970s, a professor noticed Primitivo in Puglia looked similar; in 1994, DNA showed they were identical. Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis then searched Croatia; in 2001 she confirmed Crljenak Kaštelanski as the same grape, and later found an older name, Tribidrag, recorded in the 15th century.

Since the EU and the US recognised them as the same, Italian producers can label Primitivo as Zinfandel when exporting to the US, and US producers can call theirs Primitivo. Still, the two are made in different styles: Puglian Primitivo tends to be softer and more rustic; Californian Zinfandel bolder and fruitier.
Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis led the DNA research in Croatia.

Tribidrag was mentioned in Croatian documents from the 1400s. Phylloxera and neglect almost wiped it out there. Since the DNA discovery, Croatian producers have replanted it on the Dalmatian coast. It's a reminder that wine grapes travel and change names along the way.
Zinfandel was originally an American grape.
Not true. DNA shows it came from Croatia, where it was known as Tribidrag.
DNA showed Zinfandel and Primitivo are identical in 1994
Its Croatian origin, Tribidrag, was confirmed in 2001
Labelling rules allow both names, though styles differ
Explain why old Zinfandel vines matter

Some Californian Zinfandel vineyards date from the 1880s, having survived phylloxera and Prohibition. During Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, Zinfandel was popular with home winemakers, so many vines were kept. Old, head-trained vines give low yields and concentrated, balanced fruit. Lodi and Sonoma have many.

Many old Zinfandel vineyards are field blends: Zinfandel interplanted with Petite Sirah, Carignan, Alicante Bouschet, Mourvèdre and others. Grapes are picked and fermented together. Petite Sirah adds colour and tannin, Carignan acidity. These mixed vineyards reflect how 19th century immigrants planted.
Which grapes are often found in old Zinfandel field blends?
Riesling isn't part of these red field blends.

The Historic Vineyard Society, founded in 2011, records Californian vineyards planted at least 50 years ago that still produce. It has helped protect old Zinfandel vineyards from being replanted with more profitable grapes. Producers like Ridge, Turley and Bedrock champion them.
Match each term to its meaning.
California's old vines are a living archive.
Many Californian Zinfandel vines date from the 1880s
Old vineyards are often field blends with Petite Sirah and Carignan
The Historic Vineyard Society protects them

Zinfandel's ripe fruit, spice and alcohol suit barbecue, smoked meats, burgers, sausages and sweet, spicy glazes. Its fruit handles a little sweetness in sauces. Primitivo suits Puglian food: orecchiette with sausage, grilled meats and aged cheeses. Avoid very hot chilli, which clashes with high alcohol.

In 1975, Sutter Home's fermentation stuck, leaving a sweet pink wine. It was sold as White Zinfandel and became the best-selling wine in the US in the 1980s. Its success kept many old Zinfandel vines alive, though it's very different from red Zinfandel.
A stuck fermentation that left sugar
Sutter Home's 1975 fermentation stopped, leaving a sweet pink wine that became a hit.
Serve big, high-alcohol Zinfandel slightly cool, around 16 degrees. A little chill keeps the alcohol from feeling hot.
White Zinfandel's success helped keep old Zinfandel vines in the ground.
Yes. Demand for grapes saved many vineyards from being replanted.
Zinfandel suits barbecue and sweet, spicy glazes
White Zinfandel began with a stuck fermentation in 1975
